docs.title: What are we doing here?
docs.text:
Our goal is to provide the Greek student community with a Linux distribution that will be tailored to their needs. That's why we made UniOS a free and open source Arch Linux distribution and many apps to go along with it.

In those docs you will find the technical explanation for our project; we will explain the architecture and the building pipeline of the OS and of the apps that go along with it. If you want something a bit more light-hearted that targets to explain to a non-technical friend or colleague, you can visit our webpage.

docs.title: Current list of projects
docs.text:
As of now we have developed the following projects:

  • UniOS – The repository that hosts our ISO code
  • UniBackpack – Our downloader for the software used by the departments of the Greek universities to teach each subject.
  • UniDesk – Our welcomer and helper app that runs on startup to greet the user and make them engage with our community.
  • UniMate – Our web app that serves as a bulk downloader for general use Linux apps.
  • UniNews – Our app that acts as a news aggregator for university news.
  • UniOS Update – An interactive update notifier & applier for UniOS.
  • UniNews – Our app that acts as a news aggregator for university news.
  • unios-update – An interactive update notifier & applier for UniOS that assists you with important pre / post update tasks (including a systray applet and extensive CLI).
  • unios-calamares – Our system installer
  • unios-desktop-settingss – Our scripts to make KDE feel like UniOS
  • Our Webpage – This is our landing page that does a less technical introduction for our ecosystem.
  • The webpage that you are currently on – This is our documentation page that should be considered part of the workflow if you want to write for us, which we dearly suggest.

docs.title: Our current repo:
docs.text: Our current repository that runs of github is unios-repo and you can add it in your current Linux installation following the guide in our unios-repo page.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: UniOS Landing Page is a webpage about UniOS, an operating system designed specifically for university students. It contains information about the apps included, the members of the team who created it and some frequently asked questions about it. Moreover, visitors can download the ISO of UniOS and visit the project's documentation website. It's purpose is to familiarize visitors with UniOS.

docs.title: As a user
docs.text: Because is a webpage, users don't have to install it. If they want to visit this landing page, they can click here: https://unios-project.eu

docs.title: As a developer
docs.text:
As a developer, you have to follow these steps: - Make a fork of this repository. - Clone your fork locally. - Run the project with this command:

`python3 -m http.server 8000`

_Note: To run this command, you need to have python installed._

docs.title: Project structure
docs.text: The structure of the project is this: bash . ├── assets │   ├── css │   ├── fonts │   ├── images │   ├── js │   ├── logo │   ├── members │   └── mockup ├── index.html ├── LICENSE ├── locales ├── README.md └── vendor ├── bootstrap └── jquery

docs.title: How to modify this project
docs.text:
• To change the html code, modify the index.html.
  • To change the css code, modify the unios_theme.css file.
  • To modify the webpage's text, first edit the values in 'en.json' and 'el.json', which are the webpage’s translation dictionaries, and then update the corresponding HTML elements. These dictionaries are located in the locales folder. 'en.json' contains the English text, and 'el.json' contains the Greek text.

  • To add text to the webpage, you have to follow these steps:

    • Add a key-value pair to both el.json and en.json, with the new text in Greek and English respectively. For instance:

    • en.json: "your_translation_key" : "text in english",

    • el.json: "your_translation_key" : "text in greek",

    • Add the data-i18n attribute to the HTML element containing this text, and set it to the corresponding key. For example:

      <element data-i18n="your_translation_key">...</element> - Add your text to the corresponding html element, for backup.

docs.title: Contributing
docs.text:
Contributions are welcome. If you want to improve the UI, fix a typo, or add a new page, open a pull request on GitHub. If you find a bug, open an issue. There is no contribution too small.

docs.title: build.unios.project.eu
docs.text: As mentioned in general workflow this is out build server, it is our way to maintain a coherence among the building environments of our developers and contributors. This doc is mostly directed at our core members but who knows, you might need it one day.

docs.title: How to access the server
docs.text: if you want to get your greedy little hands to our supreme computing powerhouse (20EUR VPS) you'll need to talk with the core team throught the channels listed here and get your self an SSH key, after that sends the YOUR_SSH_KEY.pub and we'll add it in the ssh keys that can access the server.

docs.title: General overview of the server
docs.text:
The build server has three accounts

  • root (We don't mess with him)

  • pkgbuilder (The account that handles the building of the packages)

  • isobuilder (The account that triggers the ISO update every month)

You will mostly interface with the pkgbuilder@build.unios-project.eu since the root is off limits and the isobuilder is mostly automated.

docs.title: pkgbuilder
docs.text:
Here we explain the workflow to build or test the changes that you made in our repos through the server. There is a repo called unios-build-autmation-scripts that contains a few scripts that automate the building process of the packages.

To update a package in unios-repo with recent changes you will utilize unios-build-automation-scripts/src/build.sh you will append the name of the package that you want to update and the process will go through mostly automatically, the only thing that you will need is the passphrase for the sighning key that will be given to you upon issueing access to the server.

To test a branch of package that you are making, well more specifically to test the binary .pkg.tar.zst you will follow the same exacty process but you will appened the branch that you want to build and then the process will continue the same as above.

docs.title: REMEMBER: Once you use the build.sh you are actually uploading directly to production (uios-repo) and your changes will be directly avaiable to our users, so please make sure that you tested your package and utilize the test.sh alongside with repo-specific testing procedures.

docs.title: General Workflow for developing UniOS or UniOS apps
docs.text: This document explains the general workflow of how to develop for UniOS and the apps that support it.

docs.title: Building process
docs.text: Because we want to build process to be as accessible to the core team without having to switch OS and developer's computer agnostic to avoid silly bugs we do maintain a server that builds the ISO and the packages, that server is build.unios-project.eu, it is accessible only through the core team members listed on our webpage, you can of course ask a maintainer to perform the build for you but in general the maintainers already know that if an issue is flagged with the build.unios-project.eu label it is to be built using the server. There is a dedicated article that details to building process on the server.

docs.title: UniOS Apps
docs.text:
In general all development and especially apps are developed via issues, the following diagram explains the workflow visually:

Namely the steps can be reduced to:

  • Issue is being created by the UniOS team or the individual

  • An individual or a team member creates a new branch and tries to solve the issue

  • After submitting the pull request and after the reviews and adjustments the PR is accepted

  • If the change is significant (marked by the significant tag in the issue page) the change should be documented in UniDocs and pushed through a PR.

  • If the change is bumping a version number, then a release should be created and a changelog should be generated.

docs.title: How to get help throughout the process
docs.text:
If you need to ask questions or need human support during the development process there are serveral ways to get it. Namely:

  • You can of course ask for help in the PR and a maintainer will get back to you as soon as possible.

  • You can ping the core team in Discord and ask them the relevant question

  • You can hop on the engineering call every Thursday with the core team of the project. (Hours vary every Thursday because we are students)

  • You can come and ask us in the office B-102 in University of Macedonia every Sunday.

docs.title: UniOS
docs.text:
Since UniOS is an Arch derivative it should be regulary updated, once every month we trigger an update and the ISO is being updated with the newest Arch packages and the newest UniOS packages. This date is set to be the 16th of every month.

We use the same server aforementioned to build the ISO, but this job is automated so there is no need for a maintainer or a contributor to do anything

In general we don't trigger "emergency" updates for bugs that are encoutered but there is a way to patch a problem in the middle of the updates interval. You can ass your fix as a dependency in the unios-applications-meta package and it will be pushed as an upgrade.

docs.title: Installing UniOS
docs.text: This guide walks you through downloading UniOS, putting it on a USB stick and installing it on your computer. No Linux experience needed, if you can install a game you can install UniOS.

docs.title: Before you start
docs.text:
Make sure your computer meets the minimum requirements:

  • A 64-bit (x86-64) computer, Apple Silicon Macs and ARM laptops are not supported
  • At least 2 CPU cores
  • At least 4GB of RAM
  • At least 25GB of free storage
  • A USB stick of 8GB or more (everything on it will be erased, unless you use Ventoy, see below)
  • An internet connection is recommended during the installation

docs.title: REMEMBER: Installing an operating system can erase your disk. Back up anything important (documents, photos, university projects) to an external drive or the cloud before you continue.
1. Download the ISO
docs.text:
Head to our download server and grab the newest .iso file (the name contains the release date, e.g. UniOS-2026.09.24-x86_64.iso):

download.unios-project.eu

You can also use the download button on our webpage. The file is about 4GB, so give it a few minutes. We publish a new ISO every month (see General Dev Workflow), but an older ISO is fine too, the system updates itself after the installation.

docs.title: 2. Make a bootable USB
docs.text: Pick one of the following tools.

docs.title: Ventoy (recommended, Windows & Linux)
docs.text:
Ventoy lets you keep many ISOs on one stick, and you just copy the .iso file onto it like any other file.

  1. Download Ventoy and run Ventoy2Disk.exe (Windows) or VentoyGUI (Linux)
  2. Select your USB stick and click Install. If the stick already has files you want to keep and is formatted as NTFS, use Option → Non-destructive Install instead
  3. Copy UniOS-....iso onto the stick

docs.title: Rufus (Windows)
docs.text:
1. Download Rufus and open it
  2. Select your USB stick under Device and the UniOS ISO under Boot selection
  3. Click Start, if Rufus asks, choose Write in DD Image mode

docs.title: balenaEtcher (Windows, macOS & Linux)
docs.text:
1. Download balenaEtcher and open it
  2. Flash from file → pick the ISO, Select target → pick the USB stick, then Flash!

docs.title: dd (Linux, for the terminal enjoyers)
docs.text:
Find your stick with lsblk and double check the name, dd will happily overwrite your main disk if you tell it to:

sudo dd if=UniOS-2026.09.24-x86_64.iso of=/dev/sdX bs=4M status=progress oflag=sync

docs.title: 3. Boot from the USB
docs.text:
1. Plug in the stick and restart the computer
  2. Open the boot menu by pressing the right key as soon as the computer turns on, it is usually one of F12, F11, F10, F8, Esc or F2 depending on the manufacturer (Dell/Lenovo: F12, HP: F9 or Esc, ASUS: F8 or Esc, Acer: F12)
  3. Select your USB stick (if you see it twice, prefer the one that says UEFI)
  4. If you used Ventoy, pick the UniOS ISO from the Ventoy menu and choose Boot in normal mode

If the computer refuses to boot the stick or shows a "Secure Boot violation" message, go into the BIOS/UEFI settings (usually F2 or Del at startup) and disable Secure Boot, then try again.

docs.title: 4. Try it out (Live session)
docs.text: UniOS will start in a live session straight from the USB, you will be logged in automatically and nothing has been changed on your computer yet. Feel free to look around, check that Wi-Fi, sound and your screen work properly before installing.

docs.title: 5. Install UniOS
docs.text:
Start the installer by double clicking Install UniOS on the desktop (it may also open by itself when the live session starts). The installer will guide you through the following:

  1. Language: choose the language of the system
  2. Location: choose your region and time zone (e.g. Europe/Athens)
  3. Keyboard: choose your keyboard layout, you can test it in the text box
  4. Partitions: choose where UniOS will be installed
    • Erase disk: UniOS takes over the whole disk, the simplest option, everything on that disk is deleted
    • Install alongside: keeps your current system (e.g. Windows) and lets you choose between them on every boot
    • Manual partitioning: for people who know what they are doing
  5. Users: your name, username, computer name and password. Don't forget your password, you will need it to install apps and updates
  6. Summary: check everything one last time and click Install

The installation takes 10 to 30 minutes depending on your computer. When it finishes, check Restart now, click Done and unplug the USB stick when the screen goes black.

docs.title: Dual booting with Windows
docs.text:
If you chose Install alongside, do the following in Windows before installing:

  • Disable Fast Startup (Control Panel → Power Options → Choose what the power buttons do)
  • If BitLocker is enabled, write down your recovery key or suspend BitLocker, Windows may ask for it after the installation
  • Make sure you have enough free space on the disk (at least 25GB) for UniOS

docs.title: 6. First boot
docs.text:
After the restart, log in with the user you created. UniDesk will greet you and help you set up the system for your university and department. From there on:

  • Install the software your courses need with UniBackpack
  • Keep up with the news of your university using UniNews
  • Keep your system up to date with unios-update, it will notify you from the system tray when updates are available

docs.title: Want to try it in a virtual machine first?
docs.text:
You can test UniOS without touching your computer using VirtualBox:

  1. Create a new VM, type Linux, version Arch Linux (64-bit)
  2. Give it at least 4GB of RAM, 2 CPUs and a 25GB disk
  3. In Settings → System, tick Enable EFI
  4. In Settings → Storage, attach the UniOS ISO to the optical drive and start the VM
  5. After the installation, remove the ISO from the optical drive before rebooting

docs.title: Something went wrong?
docs.text: Don't panic, come and talk to us! You can find us on Discord, open an issue on GitHub or visit us in office B-102 of the University of Macedonia every Sunday. See General Dev Workflow for all the ways to reach us.

docs.title: UniBackpack
docs.text: UniBackpack is a lightweight C++ Qt application designed to automate the installation of essential software and development tools for university students. By selecting the target University and Department, the application automatically detects the underlying Linux distribution's package manager (apt or pacman) and installs the required toolchain.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
Before building UniBackpack, ensure that the following dependencies are installed on your system:

  • A C++17 compatible compiler (gcc or clang)
  • CMake (version 3.10 or higher)
  • Qt6 Development Libraries
  • Polkit (pkexec) for granting installation privileges

docs.title: Installing Dependencies
docs.text:
For Arch Linux / Manjaro / EndeavourOS:

sudo pacman -S base-devel cmake qt6-base qt6-tools polkit

UniOS Logo For Debian / Ubuntu / Linux Mint:

sudo apt install build-essential cmake qt6-base-dev qt6-tools-dev-tools policykit-1

docs.title: Project Structure
docs.text:
• src/ - C++ source files (.cpp)
  • include/ - C++ header files (.hpp)
  • ui/ - Qt Designer forms (.ui)
  • resources/lists/ - Configuration files containing the software lists tailored for each academic department.
  • resources/icons/ - Icons for each academic department.

docs.title: UniDesk
docs.text: UniDesk is the welcome application that ships with UniOS, a custom Linux distribution built for students and staff for all greek universities. It gives users a friendly starting point when they boot into the system, with quick access to information about the project, useful links, and the people behind it.

docs.title: What it does
docs.text: When you open UniDesk you land on a simple screen with a two column layout. On the left you have introductory pages like Features, Links, and FAQ. On the right you have community oriented pages like Source Code, Contribute, and Credits. Clicking any button takes you to a dedicated page, and a back button always brings you home.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
Python 3.10 or newer and PyQt6.

pip install -r requirements.txt

docs.title: Running it
docs.text:
Set up a virtual environment and install the package:

python3 -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate  # On Windows: .venv\Scripts\activate
pip install -e .

Then run:

unidesk

docs.title: Project structure
docs.text:
src/unidesk/
    main.py                   entry point
    helpers/
        text_data.py          loads the text below from the bundled JSON
        academic_config.py    reads/writes the shared academic profile
        autostart.py          manages launching UniDesk at login
    ui/
        main_window.py        main window and all navigation logic
        widgets.py            shared widget helpers
        pages/                builders for each page (text, links, credits, academic config)
    styles/
        loader.py             loads the bundled .qss stylesheets and assets
        check.svg             checkmark icon for checkboxes
        widgets/
            controls.qss      buttons, checkbox and combo box roles
            labels.qss        label text roles
            layout.qss        backgrounds for windows, bars, cards and dividers
    assets/text_data/
        pages.json            body text for each informational page
        faq.json              FAQ entries as question/answer pairs
        credits.json          list of contributors
        links.json            external links shown in the Links page
        navigation.json       nav button labels and footer links
        ui_strings.json       buttons, titles and other interface text
        academic_institutions.json  known universities and their departments

All user-facing text lives in assets/text_data/. To update page content edit pages.json; to add a contributor edit credits.json. No Python changes are needed to change copy.

docs.title: Academic profile
docs.text: The footer on the home screen has a Configure UniOS button. It opens a page where you pick your university and department from dropdowns, which is saved to ~/.unios/academicConfig.json. Other UniOS apps (such as UniBackpack) read this file, so the available choices live in assets/text_data/academic_institutions.json and must stay in sync with those apps. If UniBackpack adds new universities or departments, mirror them in assets/text_data/academic_institutions.json.

docs.title: Contributing
docs.text:
Contributions are welcome. If you want to improve the UI, fix a typo, or add a new page, open a pull request on GitHub. If you find a bug, open an issue. There is no contribution too small.

Built by Open Source UoM 2026

docs.title: 1. Introduction
docs.text:
UniNews is a desktop application designed to aggregate news, announcements, and updates from universities into a single interface.

University information is often distributed across multiple sources, including RSS feeds, departmental websites, faculty announcements, and institution-wide news portals. As a result, students, researchers, and staff must frequently navigate several websites to remain informed.

UniNews addresses this problem by collecting content from multiple sources and presenting it through a unified desktop application.

The application is developed in Python using PyQt6 and follows a modular architecture that supports both RSS feeds and custom website scrapers.

docs.title: 2. Objectives
docs.text:
The primary objectives of UniNews are:

  • Centralize university-related news.
  • Reduce the effort required to monitor multiple websites.
  • Provide a clean and modern desktop experience.
  • Support extensibility through community-contributed scrapers.
  • Enable offline access to previously retrieved articles.
  • Provide configurable notifications for new content.

docs.title: 3. System Architecture
docs.text: The system consists of five major components:

docs.title: User Interface Layer
docs.text:
Responsible for:

  • Displaying articles
  • Searching articles
  • Filtering content
  • Managing settings
  • Presenting notifications

Implemented using:

  • PyQt6

docs.title: Data Acquisition Layer
docs.text:
Responsible for collecting news from external sources.

Supports:

  • RSS feeds
  • Custom HTML scrapers

Implemented using:

  • feedparser
  • requests
  • BeautifulSoup

docs.title: Scraper Framework
docs.text:
Provides a standardized mechanism for integrating new content sources.

Each scraper inherits from a common base class and returns articles in a unified format.

docs.title: Persistence Layer
docs.text:
Responsible for:

  • Storing articles
  • Storing settings
  • Preventing duplicate entries

Implemented using:

  • SQLite

docs.title: Notification Layer
docs.text:
Responsible for desktop notifications whenever new articles are discovered.

Implemented using:

  • Plyer

docs.title: 4. Article Data Model
docs.text:
All sources are normalized into a common structure.

{
    "university": str,
    "source": str,
    "title": str,
    "summary": str,
    "link": str,
    "published": str,
    "fetched_at": str,
    "image_url": str
}

This allows RSS feeds and HTML scrapers to be handled identically by the application.

docs.title: 5. RSS Feed Support
docs.text:
RSS feeds are defined in:

data/feeds.json

Example:

{
  "name": "MIT News",
  "type": "rss",
  "url": "https://news.mit.edu/rss/feed"
}

The RSS service retrieves entries and converts them into the internal article format.

docs.title: 6. Scraper Framework
docs.text:
Scrapers are located inside:

scrapers/

Each scraper extends the abstract BaseScraper class.

Example:

class ExampleScraper(BaseScraper):

    def scrape(self):
        return []

Scrapers are registered through:

SCRAPER_REGISTRY

This design allows contributors to add support for new universities without modifying the rest of the system.

docs.title: 7. University of Macedonia Integration
docs.text:
The initial scraper implementation targets the University of Macedonia.

Supported sources include:

  • Main university news
  • Departmental announcements
  • Faculty-specific news pages

The scraper supports multiple subpages and categorizes articles by source.

Examples:

  • UoM Main News
  • UoM Applied Informatics
  • UoM Economics
  • UoM Business Administration

This categorization enables filtering directly from the application interface.

docs.title: 8. Local Storage
docs.text:
UniNews stores information locally within:

local_data/

Contents include:

docs.title: SQLite Database
docs.text:
Stores:

  • Articles
  • Sources
  • Metadata

docs.title: Settings File
docs.text:
Stores:

  • Theme preferences
  • Refresh intervals
  • Notification preferences
  • Cache limits

docs.title: 9. Search and Filtering
docs.text: The application provides:

docs.title: Global Search
docs.text:
Allows users to search:

  • Article titles
  • Article summaries
  • Source names

docs.title: Source Filtering
docs.text:
Users may filter content by:

  • University
  • Department
  • Individual source

This functionality is exposed through the sidebar navigation panel.

docs.title: 10. Notifications
docs.text:
The notification subsystem supports:

  • Desktop notifications
  • Keyword-based filtering
  • Optional startup refreshes
  • Periodic automatic refreshes

Users may define keywords that trigger notifications when matched within article content.

docs.title: 11. User Interface
docs.text:
The application follows a card-based design.

Key interface components include:

docs.title: Header
docs.text:
Displays:

  • Application title
  • Refresh controls

docs.title: Sidebar
docs.text:
Provides:

  • University filtering
  • Department filtering
  • Search functionality

docs.title: Article View
docs.text:
Displays:

  • Article image
  • Title
  • Source
  • Publication date
  • Summary

docs.title: Settings Dialog
docs.text:
Allows users to configure:

  • Theme
  • Refresh interval
  • Notification preferences
  • Cache settings

docs.title: 12. Extensibility
docs.text:
UniNews has been designed with extensibility as a primary goal.

New universities can be integrated through:

docs.title: RSS Feed Integration
docs.text:
Adding a new entry to:

feeds.json

docs.title: Scraper Integration
docs.text:
Implementing:

BaseScraper

and registering it within:

SCRAPER_REGISTRY

No modifications to the user interface or database layer are required.

docs.title: 13. Future Work
docs.text:
Planned enhancements include:

  • Additional university integrations
  • Improved image caching
  • Pagination support
  • Plugin-based scraper loading
  • OPML feed import/export
  • Article bookmarking
  • Automatic update checks
  • Native Linux package distribution
  • Cross-platform installers

docs.title: 14. License
docs.text:
UniNews is released under the GNU General Public License v3.0 (GPL-3.0).

The project is maintained as an open-source initiative and welcomes community contributions.

docs.title: unios-desktop-settings
docs.text:
unios-desktop-settings is the package that gives UniOS its look on KDE Plasma. It ships the UniOS wallpapers and logo, sets Breeze Dark as the default theme, replaces the Plasma Welcome Center with our own first login setup, and puts the UniOS logo on the application launcher.

It has no code of its own to build; everything it installs is described in the PKGBUILD.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. On install, the wallpapers go to /usr/share/wallpapers/UniOS, so they show up in Plasma's wallpaper picker as UniOS Wallpapers, and the logo replaces the KDE start-here and distributor icons.
  2. System-wide defaults in /etc/xdg make Breeze Dark the look and feel, color scheme, icon theme and Plasma theme.
  3. The Plasma Welcome Center is turned off, both through its autostart entry and through the defaults in /etc/skel that every new user gets.
  4. On every login, the unios-plasma-setup.sh autostart script waits for Plasma to start, sets default.jpg as the wallpaper of every desktop, and sets the UniOS logo as the icon of the application launcher on every panel.

Since the files in /etc/skel are only copied when a user is created, existing users keep their Welcome Center settings. The theme defaults in /etc/xdg apply to anyone who hasn't changed them in their own ~/.config.

docs.title: As a user
docs.text:
On UniOS, unios-desktop-settings is preinstalled. If you removed it, install it again from unios-repo:

sudo pacman -S unios-desktop-settings

On other Arch-based distributions running KDE Plasma, build the package from the PKGBUILD in this repository:

git clone https://github.com/open-source-uom/unios-desktop-settings.git
cd unios-desktop-settings
makepkg -si

Log out and back in afterwards, so the setup script runs.

docs.title: As a developer
docs.text:
You only need base-devel and a KDE Plasma session to test the result:

sudo pacman -S base-devel

Build the package without installing it, and check what it would install:

makepkg -f
tar -tf unios-desktop-settings-*.pkg.tar.zst

When you're happy with it, install it with makepkg -si and log in again. To build it for unios-repo, follow the pkgbuilder process in our build server docs.

docs.title: Project Structure
docs.text:
unios-desktop-settings/
├── PKGBUILD                  package recipe; also generates every config file below
├── resources/
│   ├── logos/
│   │   └── unios.png         the UniOS logo
│   └── wallpapers/
│       ├── default.jpg       the wallpaper set on login
│       ├── dense_repeating_patterns.jpg
│       └── repeating_patterns.jpg
└── .github/workflows/
    └── publish_to_PPA.yml    leftover from the Debian packaging

docs.title: Files the package installs
docs.text:
Path What it is /usr/share/wallpapers/UniOS/contents/images/ every image in resources/, except the logo /usr/share/wallpapers/UniOS/metadata.json names the wallpaper pack UniOS Wallpapers /usr/share/pixmaps/unios.png the UniOS logo /usr/share/icons/hicolor/.../apps/ the logo as unios, start-here-kde and distributor-logo /etc/xdg/kdeglobals Breeze Dark look and feel, color scheme and icons /etc/xdg/plasmarc Breeze Dark Plasma theme /etc/skel/.config/plasma-welcome-appletsrc hides the Welcome Center for new users /etc/skel/.config/kded_plasma_welcomerc stops the Welcome Center daemon module for new users /usr/lib/unios/unios-plasma-setup.sh the login setup script /etc/xdg/autostart/unios-plasma-setup.desktop runs the setup script on login /etc/xdg/autostart/org.kde.plasma-welcome.desktop hides the Welcome Center autostart entry

For example, /etc/xdg/kdeglobals looks like this:

[KDE]
LookAndFeelPackage=org.kde.breezedark.desktop

[General]
ColorScheme=BreezeDark

[Icons]
Theme=breeze-dark

docs.title: The setup script
docs.text:
unios-plasma-setup.sh uses qdbus6 (or qdbus, if that's what's available) to talk to plasmashell. It tries for up to 15 seconds until Plasma answers, then runs a Plasma script that:

  • sets /usr/share/wallpapers/UniOS/contents/images/default.jpg on every desktop
  • finds every Kickoff, Kicker or app menu widget on every panel and sets /usr/share/pixmaps/unios.png as its icon

Finally it applies the wallpaper once more with plasma-apply-wallpaperimage. It runs in autostart phase 2, after the desktop and panels have loaded, and it doesn't write anything outside of Plasma's own config.

docs.title: Adding a Wallpaper
docs.text:
1. Put the image in resources/wallpapers/. .jpg, .jpeg, .png and .webp files are picked up.
  2. Don't put logo in its name; those files are treated as the logo and left out of the wallpapers.
  3. To change the wallpaper that is set on login, replace default.jpg, since that name is hardcoded in the setup script.
  4. Bump pkgrel in the PKGBUILD (or pkgver, and reset pkgrel to 1) so users get the update.

docs.title: Changing the Logo
docs.text: Replace resources/logos/unios.png. The first file named unios.png, or with logo in its name, is used, so keep a single one in resources/.

docs.title: Recent Changes
docs.text:
• UniOS moved to Arch, so the Debian packaging and the Launchpad PPA were dropped in favour of a PKGBUILD. The publish_to_PPA.yml workflow is still in the repository, but it can no longer build anything without the debian/ folder.
  • Wallpapers and the logo moved to resources/wallpapers/ and resources/logos/, and new wallpapers were added.
  • The Plasma Welcome Center is now hidden through its autostart entry and the /etc/skel defaults.

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
An interactive update notifier & applier for UniOS that assists you with important pre / post update tasks. Includes a systray applet for an easy integration with any desktop / graphical environment. You will see a lot of referals to Arch Linux because UniOS is a respin. This notifier is the one Arch Linux uses with stylistic changes to fit our operating system.

UniOS-Update is designed to follow usual system maintenance steps, as described in the Arch Wiki.

Features:

  • Automatic check and listing of available updates.
  • Check for recent Arch Linux news (and offers to display them if there are).
  • Check for orphan packages (and offers to remove them if there are).
  • Check for old & uninstalled packages in cache (and offers to remove them if there are).
  • Check for pacnew & pacsave files (and offers to process them if there are).
  • Check for pending kernel update requiring a reboot (and offers to do so if there's one).
  • Check for services requiring a post upgrade restart (and offers to do so if there are).
  • Support for sudo, sudo-rs, doas & run0.
  • Extensive CLI.

Optional support for:

  • Flatpak packages (via flatpak).
  • Desktop notifications (via libnotify).
  • Check for ALHP build queue or outdated mirrors (via alhp-utils).

docs.title: From Source
docs.text:
Install required runtime dependencies:

sudo pacman -S --needed bash systemd pacman pacman-contrib archlinux-contrib glibc libgcc curl fakeroot htmlq diffutils hicolor-icon-theme glib2 xdg-utils util-linux

Additional optional dependencies you might want or need:

  • flatpak: Flatpak Packages support
  • libnotify: Desktop notifications support on new available updates (see https://wiki.archlinux.org/title/Desktop_notifications)
  • alhp-utils: Check for ALHP build queue or outdated mirrors
  • vim: Default diff program for pacdiff
  • neovim: Default diff program for pacdiff if EDITOR=nvim
  • sudo: Privilege elevation
  • sudo-rs: Privilege elevation
  • opendoas: Privilege elevation

Install required build and test dependencies:

sudo pacman -S --asdeps make scdoc bats cargo pkgconf

Download the archive of the latest stable release and extract it (alternatively, you can clone this repository with git).

To build and install unios-update, go into the extracted / cloned directory and run the following commands:

make # You can optionally pass the `WITH_TRAY=false` argument to not build the systray applet
make test
sudo make install # You can optionally pass the `WITH_TRAY=false` argument to not install the systray applet

Once the installation is complete, you may optionally clean up the directory of files generated during installation by running the following command:

make clean

To uninstall unios-update, go into the extracted / cloned directory and run the following command:

sudo make uninstall

docs.title: Usage
docs.text: For desktop machines, the usage consist of starting the systray applet and enabling the automated update checks. For headless machines, UniOS-Update includes an extensive CLI.

docs.title: The systray applet
docs.text:
To start the systray applet and enable it automatically at boot, run the following command (preferred method for most environments, uses XDG Autostart):

unios-update --tray --enable

In case your graphical environment doesn't support XDG Autostart, add the following command your environment auto-start method instead:

Note that the small startup delay in the form of the sleep 3 command may not always be required but acts as a useful trick to avoid eventual race condition issues which may lead to the systray applet unexpectedly not starting at boot. I therefore recommend its usage as a safety measure (this small delay is already applied by default with the XDG Autostart / unios-update --tray --enable method).

sleep 3 && unios-update --tray

The systray icon dynamically changes to indicate the current state of your system ('up to date' or 'updates available'). When clicked, it launches unios-update in a terminal window via the unios-update.desktop file. The systray applet menu shows further information (like the list of pending updates, time of the last and next checks, ...) and allows to trigger specific actions (like running UniOS-Update, check for updates, ...). See screenshots for more details.

Notes:

  • GNOME shell does not support systray icons natively, GNOME users need to install the "AppIndicator and KStatusNotifierItem Support" extension for the systray applet to work.

docs.title: The automated update checks
docs.text:
To enable automated and periodic checks for available updates, run the following command:

unios-update --check --enable

By default, a check is performed at boot and then once every 6 hours. The check cycle can be customized, see this chapter.

docs.title: Screenshots
docs.text:
Once started, the systray applet appears in the systray area of your panel. It is the third icon on the left in the screenshot below:

On hover if there are new available updates, the systray icon shows a notification indicating the number of available updates. You can click on it and run UniOS-Update:

When the systray icon is left-clicked, unios-update is run in a terminal window

From there, just let UniOS-Update guide you through the various steps required for a complete and proper update of your system! :smile:

Certain options can be enabled, disabled or modified via the unios-update.conf configuration file. See the unios-update.conf(5) man page for more details.

docs.title: unios-update
docs.text: See unios-update --help and the unios-update(1) man page.

docs.title: unios-update configuration file
docs.text: See the unios-update.conf(5) man page.

docs.title: Modify the check cycle
docs.text:
If you enabled the automated update checks, a check for available updates is automatically launched at boot and then once each 6 hours.

If you want to customize the check cycle, run systemctl --user edit --full unios-update.timer and modify the OnUnitActiveSec value to your liking. For instance, if you want UninOS-Update to check for new updates every 4 hours instead:

[...]
[Timer]
OnStartupSec=15
OnUnitActiveSec=4h
[...]

Time units are s for seconds, m for minutes, h for hours, d for days... See https://www.freedesktop.org/software/systemd/man/latest/systemd.time.html#Parsing%20Time%20Spans for more details.

In case you want UniOS-Update to check for new updates only once at boot, you can simply delete the OnUnitActiveSec line completely.
